title: Launchpad
teaches: The launchpad as we trade it: after a real correction a stock rests five weeks or more under three averages pinched within 3% of price near a flat 200-day, the launch bar closes above all four averages up 2% or more in the top of its range, the stop sits a few cents under the launch day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the 21-day trail, and the stock, the base and the market, not the bar, carry the edge.

facts.quote: The Launch Pad Setup occurs when price reclaims important KMAs to the upside on volume.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the Launch Pad is price reclaiming its key moving averages on volume.

facts.quote: Price trades underneath the KMAs in a base
facts.claim: TraderLion step one: price trades underneath the key averages in a base.

facts.quote: Price reclaims these KMAs to the upside
facts.claim: TraderLion step two: price reclaims the averages.

facts.quote: The KMAs start to curl underneath price, forming a Launch Pad for higher prices
facts.claim: TraderLion step three: the averages curl underneath price, forming the launch pad.

facts.quote: Price retests the KMAs & bounces off of them
facts.claim: TraderLion step four: price retests the averages and bounces.

facts.quote: the Power of 3 Setup occurs when a stock goes from trading below its 10, 21, and 50-day Simple Moving Averages to trading above in a single session.
facts.claim: Rai: the Power of 3 is a stock going from below its 10, 21 and 50-day averages to above them in one session.

facts.quote: Moving averages should be horizontal as price breaks through. Downtrending MAs decrease the probability of success of the setup.
facts.claim: Rai: the averages should be horizontal as price breaks through; falling averages hurt the odds.

facts.quote: Stop techniques usually all revolve around the stock breaking below recent lows (preferably within 3-5% of entry price) or multi-day closes below the moving averages of interest.
facts.claim: Rai: stops sit under recent lows, preferably within 3 to 5% of the entry.

facts.quote: a stock's key moving averages converge to the upside in a tight bunch beneath price.
facts.claim: Haber: the key averages converge in a tight bunch beneath price.

facts.quote: Tight relative to itself. The bunch should be visibly tighter than the averages were during the prior decline or base.
facts.claim: Haber: tight means visibly tighter than the averages were during the prior decline.

facts.quote: A pile of flat averages above price is a ceiling, not a launchpad.
facts.claim: Haber: flat averages above price are a ceiling, not a launchpad.

facts.quote: A launchpad forming on an early-stage base at the start of a new uptrend carries far more weight than one forming after the stock has already doubled.
facts.claim: Haber: an early-stage launchpad carries far more weight than one after the stock has doubled.

facts.quote: Wide, loose stocks with huge average daily ranges can form something that looks like a launchpad, but it's often a trap
facts.claim: Haber: wide, loose stocks with huge daily ranges form launchpad look-alikes that are often a trap.

facts.quote: If the distance is more than 3%, the entry isn't there yet. Wait, or pass.
facts.claim: Haber: if the stop is more than 3% away, wait or pass.

facts.quote: In each bull market cycle, the strongest stocks will pause their advance, consolidate their recent gains, form a new base, and then break out to even higher levels.
facts.claim: Deepvue: the strongest stocks pause, consolidate, form a new base, then break out.

facts.quote: A protective stop can then be placed at the opposite end of the range.
facts.claim: Deepvue puts the stop at the other end of the tight range.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: a climax run on your own long: sell a big part into it.

facts.quote: Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Close of $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day on average over 50 days.
facts.claim: Liquidity: a close of $10 or more and $20 million a day over 50 days.

facts.quote: A real correction first: the lowest close of the last 60 sessions is at least 15% under the highest high of the 60 sessions before that.
facts.claim: A real correction first: the lowest close of the last 60 sessions at least 15% under the prior 60 sessions' high.

facts.quote: A long base: at least 25 sessions (5 weeks) of closes within 10% of the bundle's middle.
facts.claim: A long base: at least 25 sessions of closes within 10% of the bundle's middle.

facts.quote: The last 30 closes span no more than 20% of price.
facts.claim: The last 30 closes span no more than 20% of price.

facts.quote: Fewer than 20 of the prior 40 closes are above the highest of the three averages.
facts.claim: Fewer than 20 of the prior 40 closes sit above the highest of the three averages.

facts.claim: Tight: the bundle's three averages lie within 3% of price of each other the day before the launch.

facts.quote: The 200-day is close: within 10% of the bundle's middle on the day before the launch. Better: at or just under the bundle.
facts.claim: The 200-day is close, within 10% of the bundle's middle; better at or just under the bundle.

facts.claim: The launch bar closes above all four averages; a close inside the bundle or under the 200-day is not the launch.

facts.claim: The launch bar is up 2% or more on the day.

facts.claim: The launch bar closes in the top 35% of its range, 0.65 or higher.

facts.claim: Volume of 2 times the 50-day average is the A+ launch bar, not a rule.

facts.claim: The launch opens no more than 6% above the prior close and is not a news bar; a bigger gap is another setup.

steps: KBH, 2004. A four-month correction of 24.8%. Then two months around a flat 200-day while the averages pinch within 3%.
Context and pattern check out: a real correction, a long base, a tight bundle, the 200-day close. Now wait for the launch.
2004-09-01: up 2.5%, closing at 0.94 of its range, above all four averages. Fill 35.26; stop under the low, 34.26.

walkthroughs.title: BABA, January 2025: under the bundle, then the launch
steps: BABA, 2025. After a 31.6% correction, 26 of 40 closes sat under the bundle, none above. The 200-day is 1% away.

2025-01-24: up 3.5%, closing at its high above all four. Fill 89.14; stop a few cents under the low, 86.43.

walkthroughs.title: DDOG, October 2024: the dangle, the trail and the time stop
steps: DDOG, 2024. A 22.1% correction, a 1.66% bundle. On 2024-10-04 it launches up 4.4%, closing at 0.97, on 1.63x volume.
Fill 122.69; stop 118.32, 3.6% away. Over 3%, so the size shrinks. Never pull the stop in to fit.

questions.q: In one line, what is a launchpad?
choices: A long rest under tight averages
A box at the highs after a 30% run-up
A pole that doubles in a few weeks
A V rally up through the averages
questions.answer: A long rest under tight averages
questions.why: A long rest under tight averages, ended by a launch. After a real correction the stock rests five weeks or more with the averages pinched within 3%. The launch bar then closes above all four averages. TraderLion describes the same path: price trades underneath the averages in a base, reclaims them, and they curl underneath price. It is not a breakout over a base high.
questions.lesson_line: A launchpad is a long rest under averages that pinched together, then the day price clears them.

wrong.A box at the highs after a 30% run-up: That is closer to a flat base, which holds above the 50-day and breaks out over its own highest high.
wrong.A pole that doubles in a few weeks: A launchpad follows a 15% correction and five weeks or more under a tight bundle. It is a rest after a fall, not a surge.
wrong.A V rally up through the averages: A V rally has no long rest under the averages. A launchpad rests there for five weeks or more first.

questions.simple: A launchpad is a long rest under averages that have pinched together, ended by a day that closes above them.

reasons: the long rest and the tight bundle are the unit's proposed card lines, with TraderLion's four steps as the outside view

questions.q: What came right before this launchpad's long rest?
choices: A correction of 15% or more
A new high, volume rising
A 5% dip, then a bounce
A climb over the 50-day
questions.why: A correction of 15% or more. The lowest close of the last 60 sessions sits at least 15% under the highest high of the 60 sessions before that. A launchpad follows that fall, then rests five weeks or more under a tight bundle.
questions.lesson_line: No correction, no pad. The rest comes after the fall.

wrong.A new high, volume rising: A launchpad follows a fall, not a new high. The correction comes first, then the rest.
wrong.A 5% dip, then a bounce: Too shallow. The line is a correction of at least 15%, then weeks of rest.
wrong.A climb over the 50-day: Price riding on top of the averages in an uptrend is a pullback breakout, not a launchpad.

questions.simple: A real fall comes first, because a launchpad is the long rest after a correction of at least 15%.

reasons: the 15% line is the unit's proposed card number and the near-miss note shows a second option under review

questions.q: Which average does a launchpad's trail follow by default?
choices: The 20 EMA
The 9 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
questions.why: The 20 EMA, the steadier trail. Trail what is left on a close under the 20 EMA. Launchpads come out of long bases and tend to trend along the 20 EMA. Use the 9 EMA only if the stock is a fast mover. Our trail rule is the same split: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones. How much is left depends on the first sell, which is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: A pad trends along the 20 EMA. Trail it there and sell the close below.

wrong.The 50-day: That is not the trail. What is left trails the 20 EMA and sells on a close below it.
wrong.The 200-day: The 200-day is the line new longs must stay above, not a trail. What is left trails the 20 EMA.
wrong.The 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is for a fast mover. A pad out of a long base tends to trend along the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA is the default trail, because a launchpad out of a long base tends to trend along it.

deeper.trap: The sell signal is a close below the 20 EMA, not a dip under it during the day. Use the 9 EMA only for a fast mover.

questions.q: A textbook pad in a slow regional bank grades lower than one in a leader.
questions.why: True. Slow, heavy names grade down. We want a leader or a stock in a strong group, not a slow bank. Growing sales and earnings are preferred, but the chart comes first. CMCSA launched on big volume in a slow large cap, had one flat day, then fell back into the bundle.
questions.lesson_line: The pad is the shape. The stock is the trade.
questions.simple: True. Slow, heavy stocks grade lower, so the same pad is worth less in a slow bank than in a leader.

questions.lesson_line: The launch is the close above the averages, not a base top.
questions.simple: False. The launch is the close above the averages, so the bar can still sit inside the base.

questions.q: How long is a launchpad base, at least?
choices: 25 sessions, about five weeks
5 sessions, about one week
10 sessions, about two weeks
100 sessions, about five months
questions.why: At least 25 sessions, about five weeks, with closes within 10% of the bundle's middle. That is the floor for a launchpad base. A tight range of only a few days under the fast averages is a wedge pop, a different setup.
questions.lesson_line: Five weeks or more under the bundle. Days are a wedge pop, not a pad.

questions.q: The launch bar must be up 2% or more on the day.
questions.why: True. The launch bar is a real push: up 2% or more on the day. AIZ launched on +2.0%, the smallest launch bar of the ten examples and exactly the floor. The floor lets a stock in. It does not promise the trade works.
questions.lesson_line: A launch is a push, not a drift. Two percent is the floor.
questions.simple: True. The launch bar has to be up at least 2% on the day, so a slow drift higher does not count.

deeper.counter: A bigger push is no guarantee. The four failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, closing in the top third. Nothing on the bar separated them from the ten winners. The stock, the base and the market carry the edge.

questions.q: Where does our primary stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Just under the averages' bottom
Just under the base low
At the fill, the buy price
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the launch day's low, our primary stop. The averages' bottom and the base low are allowed stops in principle, but they usually sit further from the buy than the day's low. A stop past 5% from the buy means we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. A stop at the fill is breakeven, which comes after 2R.
questions.lesson_line: The launch day's low is the primary stop. The averages' bottom and the base low are allowed but usually sit further away.

wrong.Just under the averages' bottom: That is the bottom of the averages, an allowed stop in general, but it usually sits further from the buy than the day's low. The primary stop is under the launch day's low.
wrong.Just under the base low: That is the base low, an allowed stop in general, but it usually sits further from the buy than the day's low. The primary stop is under the launch day's low.
wrong.At the fill, the buy price: A stop at the fill is breakeven. The stop moves there once 2R has traded, not on day one.

questions.simple: The primary stop goes a few cents under the launch day's low. The averages' bottom and the base low usually sit further away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13 stop habit, D41, A4)

questions.simple: True. We hold through an earnings report only when the trade is already up 5R.

questions.lesson_line: Tight is a number here: three percent of price across the three lines.
questions.simple: The three bundle averages must sit within 3% of price of each other, or the pad is not tight enough.

deeper.trap: The 3% is measured against price, not against one average. Take the highest of the three averages minus the lowest, divide by price, on the day before the launch.

questions.q: What do we call this?
choices: A breakout, not a launchpad
A launchpad; it cleared all four
The fastest kind of launchpad
A wedge pop off a tight range
questions.why: A breakout, not a launchpad. A V rally up into the bundle from far below is a breakout. Here the stock rallied straight up and closed above all four within a week. A launchpad rests at least 25 sessions, about five weeks, under tight averages first, and this stock had no rest. Clearing all four is the launch bar's job. The rest comes before it.
questions.lesson_line: A V into the averages is a breakout wearing a pad's name.

wrong.A launchpad; it cleared all four: Clearing all four is the launch bar's job. The pad needs weeks of rest under them first, and there were none.
wrong.The fastest kind of launchpad: Speed is no credit here. A pad is a slow rest: five weeks or more under the bundle.
wrong.A wedge pop off a tight range: A wedge pop starts from a tight range of a few days under the fast averages. This stock rallied straight up from far below.

questions.story: The stock fell 25% below its averages, then rallied straight up into them. It closed above all four within one week.
questions.simple: It is a breakout. The stock rallied straight up into the averages, and a pad rests under them for weeks first.

deeper.trap: Do not judge by the launch bar alone. A V rally can close above all four averages with a strong green bar and look just like a launch. What it lacks is the weeks of tight rest underneath. Count the sessions under the bundle before you call it a pad.

reasons: rests on the unit's card lines (c23, c03)

300,000 shares
3,000 shares
150,000 shares

questions.q: Buy at this open, or pass, and why?
choices: Pass; 5% is past the 4% limit
Pass; it fails the 6% gap rule
Buy; 5% is inside the 6% gap line
Buy half size to cut the risk
questions.why: Pass at this open. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. The open at 52.50 is 5% over the launch close of 50.00, and further over the averages at 47.00. Either way it fails. The 6% line is a different test: it limits how far the launch bar itself may open above its prior close. Chasing costs size, not risk, because the stop stays put. One more way in is a morning flush or pullback that curls back up.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy half size to cut the risk: Half of a chase is still a chase. The rule is on the price you pay, not the size.
wrong.Pass; it fails the 6% gap rule: Right to pass, wrong reason. The 6% rule limits the launch bar's own open. This entry fails the rule of never buying more than 4% above the buy point.
wrong.Buy; 5% is inside the 6% gap line: The 6% line limits how far the launch bar may open above its prior close. The entry rule is never more than 4% above the buy point.

deeper.trap: The limit is on what you pay. Chasing keeps the same stop under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. A half-size chase does not fix a price that fails the test. The 6% gap line belongs to the launch bar, not to the next morning's entry. A gap past 4% is not the end: a morning flush that curls back up is one more way in.

questions.q: Same shape. Pad A is the first one off a bottom; pad B forms after the stock has doubled. Which leans toward the higher grade?

Pad B; it is proven
Equal; same shape
Pad B; it carries momentum
questions.answer: Pad A; the run is still ahead
questions.why: Pad A. Our card says the first launchpad after the bottom grades higher than a late, repeated one. Shape is one input, and where the pad sits in the stock's cycle is another.
questions.lesson_line: The first pad out of the bottom leans higher. Late pads come after the run.

wrong.Pad B; it carries momentum: Momentum behind it means the run already happened. The card ranks the first pad after the bottom above a late, repeated one.

wrong.Sell a little and let it run: The rule says sell a big part into a climax run, not a little. How big is a judgment call.
wrong.Hold it all for the 20 EMA trail: The trail is for what is left. A climax run asks for a big sale before the trail ever triggers.

The 1.3x day; quieter is better

questions.q: A clean pad on an $8 stock trading $6 million a day on average. Take it?

Yes; a clean pad is a clean pad
Yes, but only a small size

wrong.Yes, but only a small size: Size does not make a thin stock liquid.

questions.q: Launchpad or wedge pop?

A launchpad; it cleared the averages
Neither; the fall was too deep
A flat base; the range is tight
questions.answer: A wedge pop; days, not weeks
questions.why: A wedge pop. It is a tight range of a few days under the fast averages after a decline. The pop then reclaims those two fast lines. A launchpad rests 25 sessions or more with the 8, 21 and 50-day within 3% of each other near the 200. Four days is a wedge pop's rest, not a pad's.
questions.lesson_line: Count the sessions. A pad is weeks; a wedge pop is days.

wrong.A launchpad; it cleared the averages: Clearing two fast averages after four days is the wedge pop's trigger. A pad needs weeks under all three.
wrong.Neither; the fall was too deep: Deep is fine for either. The length of the rest is what separates them.
wrong.A flat base; the range is tight: A flat base holds above the 50-day and breaks out over its own highest high. This range rested under the fast averages after a fall.

questions.story: After a 30% fall the stock holds a four-day tight range under the two fast averages, then pops over them.
questions.simple: A four-day rest is a wedge pop, because a launchpad needs weeks under pinched averages.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (wedge pop, 25-session base)

questions.q: Launchpad?

Yes; the averages pinched
Yes; above the 200-day is enough
No; a pad needs a 20% fall
questions.answer: No; the fall was too shallow
questions.why: No. A launchpad needs a real correction first. The lowest close of the last 60 sessions must be 15% or more under the prior 60-session high. Here it is 11.2% under. That is a shallow pullback over a rising 200-day, a moving-average pullback, not a pad. Pinched averages and a strong day do not make up for the missing fall.
questions.lesson_line: A shallow dip in an uptrend is a pullback trade with its own rules.

wrong.Yes; the averages pinched: Averages pinch in pullbacks too. The pad needs the correction first.
wrong.Yes; above the 200-day is enough: Above the 200-day is the context for every long. It does not make a pullback a pad.
wrong.No; a pad needs a 20% fall: 20% or deeper is the A+ cue. The gate is a correction of 15% or more, and 11.2% is under both.

questions.story: Over a rising 200-day, the lowest close of the last 60 sessions is 11.2% under the prior 60-session high. The averages pinch and a strong day closes above them.
questions.simple: No, because the fall was only 11.2% and a launchpad needs a correction of at least 15% first.

deeper.example: The tell is the order of events. A pad is a rest after a fall. A pullback is a dip inside a rising trend. This one fell 11.2% over a rising 200-day, so it was a moving-average pullback, not a pad, even with the averages pinched.

reasons: the 15% correction line is a proposed card number
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Launchpad?
choices: No; the averages were not pinched
Yes; 2.78x volume is A+
Yes; it cleared the averages
No; a 4.8% bar is too big
questions.answer: No; the averages were not pinched
questions.why: No. The averages had not converged. The three averages span 5.77% of price the day before, and the rule is 3% or less. A +4.8% bar on 2.78x volume through a loose bundle under a falling 200-day is a rally bar, not a launch. Volume grades a launch that exists. It cannot create the pad.
questions.lesson_line: No bundle, no pad. A big bar through loose averages is just a big bar.

wrong.Yes; 2.78x volume is A+: Volume grades a launch that exists. A 5.77% spread means there was no pad to launch from.
wrong.Yes; it cleared the averages: It cleared loose averages under a falling 200-day. That is a rally bar, not a launch.
wrong.No; a 4.8% bar is too big: A big bar is not a flaw: the push needs only 2% or more. The miss here is the loose averages.

questions.story: The three averages span 5.77% of price the day before. A +4.8% bar on 2.78x volume breaks through them under a falling 200-day.
questions.simple: No, because the averages were 5.77% apart and a pad needs them within 3%, so the big bar was just a rally.

deeper.trap: A big bar on big volume draws the eye. But the real test comes the day before: are the averages within 3% of each other? Here they were 5.77% apart. Skipping that test is how a rally bar gets called a launch.

reasons: the 3% bundle width is a proposed card number

questions.q: Price rode on top of the three averages before this bar. It is still a launchpad if they are tight.
questions.why: False. Price riding on top of the bundle is a pullback breakout, not a launchpad. Tight averages do not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Tight averages with price on top is a pullback. The pad has price under them.
questions.simple: False, because a pad needs price to rest under the averages, and riding on top of them is a pullback.

deeper.counter: Tight averages can still sit under price. That is price riding on top of the bundle in an uptrend, a pullback breakout. A launchpad is the other way round: its closes sit under the averages first.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (price riding on top of the bundle is a pullback breakout)

questions.q: What is the read?
choices: Right bar, wrong kind of stock
The volume lied; skip 2x bars
The stop was too tight; widen it
The 16% correction was too shallow
questions.answer: Right bar, wrong kind of stock
questions.why: Right bar, wrong kind of stock. The numbers pass: a 16% correction, a tight bundle, a push over 2% and heavy volume. But this was a slow large cap, and slow, heavy names grade down. A strong launch bar did not protect it; the stock carries the edge. The stop kept the loss at 1R, none worse.
questions.lesson_line: The bar is the timing. The stock, the base and the market are the edge.

wrong.The volume lied; skip 2x bars: Volume of 2 times the average is a cue toward A+, not a reason to skip. The loss came from the stock, a slow large cap.
wrong.The stop was too tight; widen it: A few cents under the launch low is the rule, and a stop only moves up. The stop did its job: 1R, none worse.
wrong.The 16% correction was too shallow: The rule needs a correction of 15% or more, so 16% passes. 20% or deeper is the A+ cue, which grades the pad but does not gate it.

questions.story: A 16% correction, a 0.83% bundle, a +4.9% launch on 2.17x volume in a slow large cap. One flat day, then two red days back into the bundle took the stop.
questions.simple: The launch bar looked fine, but the stock was a slow large cap, and the stop kept the loss at 1R.

deeper.trap: The bar cannot tell you the stock. The four failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, closing in the top third. A strong bar did not keep a slow large cap from failing. So read the stock first: a leader or a stock in a strong group, not a slow bank.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (stock quality, grade down for slow names)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: How many R is that?
questions.why: The gain is the exit minus the fill, 102.69 minus 89.14. One R is the fill minus the stop, 89.14 minus 86.43. The gain divided by one R is 5R. Selling at about 5 to 10R is often best, but the sell is a judgment. BABA, from this same fill, reached 3R in 3 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. About 5R to 10R is often a good place to sell.
questions.simple: The stock is 5R up, five times the distance from fill to stop, a spot where selling is often best.

deeper.trap: R is counted from the fill, not from the stop. Counting from the stop counts the risk itself as gain, so it reads one R too high. A dollar gain misleads too: it means nothing until you divide it by the risk per share. Five R is a yardstick, not an automatic sale.

reasons: +2 computed key (R multiple)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E51 plan, marked adjustable)

wrong.0.2R: That divides the gain by the price, not by R.
wrong.2.7R: That is the risk per share read as R. Divide the gain by it.
wrong.4.0R: Took one R off the gain before dividing.

questions.story: Bought on the launch day at 89.14 with the stop at 86.43. Later the stock trades to 102.69.

questions.q: Launchpad or flat base?
choices: A flat base; it broke its own high
A launchpad; averages are nearby
Both; the labels are the same
A VCP; it held a rising 50-day
questions.answer: A flat base; it broke its own high
questions.why: A flat base. It holds above the 50-day and breaks out over its own highest high. Here that is nine weeks above a rising 50-day in a box, then a trade through the top. A launchpad lives under the averages, and its launch is the close above them, not a base top.
questions.lesson_line: Look where the closes sat. Above the 50-day in a box is the flat base.

wrong.A launchpad; averages are nearby: Near is not under. A pad spends weeks under the bundle; this one never did.
wrong.Both; the labels are the same: Each has its own trigger. A pad's is the close above the averages. A flat base's is a break of its own high.
wrong.A VCP; it held a rising 50-day: A VCP shows pullbacks that shrink one after another above a rising 50-day. This is one flat box, not a run of shrinking pullbacks.

questions.story: For nine weeks every close held above a rising 50-day in a box near the highs. Today it trades through the box's top.
questions.simple: A flat base, because the stock held above its 50-day in a box and broke over the top.

deeper.counter: Look where the closes sat. A flat base holds above the 50-day and breaks out over its own highest high. A pad rests under the bundle, and its launch is the close above it.

reasons: rests on a proposed card lookalike line
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: If the first 30 minutes of a gap-down day take the loss past 2R, you get out.
questions.why: True. The first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Two R, and you are out.

questions.q: Does the time stop fire?
choices: No; over 1R, so it stays
Yes; ten days, no 3R
Yes; sell half of it
No; any gain exempts it
questions.why: No. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. This one was over 1R by day ten, so it stays. The test is 1R, not 3R. A pad that does not expand is a quiet failure, but a slow pad that is working is not. DDOG took 33 sessions to reach 3R and ran to 10.8R.
questions.lesson_line: The time stop asks for 1R, not 3R. A slow pad that is working is left alone.

wrong.Yes; ten days, no 3R: The line is 1R, not 3R. Over 1R in ten days means the trade has done something.
wrong.Yes; sell half of it: There is no half rule here. Either it is under 1R and sold, or it stays.
wrong.No; any gain exempts it: The line is 1R, not any profit. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even if it is slightly up.

questions.story: Bought on the launch day at 122.69 with the stop at 118.32. The stock dangles near its short averages for four weeks. By day ten it has traded over 1R but not 3R.
questions.simple: No, because the time stop only sells a trade still under 1R after ten days, and this one was over.

deeper.example: DDOG, launch 2024-10-04: bought 122.69, stop 118.32. It dangled near its short averages for four weeks. 3R took 33 sessions, yet it was over 1R inside 10 days. It ran to 10.8R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33 time stop)

questions.q: What happens to the rest of the position?
choices: Sold on that close under the 20 EMA
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Held until a close under the 50-day
Sold after two closes under the 20 EMA
questions.answer: Sold on that close under the 20 EMA
questions.why: Sold. What is left trails the 20 EMA, the steadier trail, and comes off on a close below it. This stock is a steady mover, so the 20 EMA is the line, and today's close under it is the exit. The 9 EMA is only for a fast mover. Breakeven is a floor, not the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Part is banked, the rest is on the trail. The close below the line is the exit.

wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven is the stop's floor, not the plan. The trail is the exit for what is left.
wrong.Held until a close under the 50-day: The trail for a steadier mover is the 20 EMA, not the 50-day.
wrong.Sold after two closes under the 20 EMA: The rule sells on a close below the 20 EMA. One close is the signal, not two.

questions.story: You have sold part of the position into strength. Today the steady mover closes under the 20 EMA for the first time since the launch.
questions.simple: Sell it, because what is left rides the 20 EMA and one close below that line is the exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52 trail)

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Yes; a new trade, new stop
No; each pad gets one try
Yes; with a wider, safer stop
No; cool off for a week first
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Here the stock closed back above all four averages, up 3%, so the launch can trigger again. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next launch is a new trade.

wrong.No; each pad gets one try: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes; with a wider, safer stop: The new trade gets its own honest stop, a few cents under the new launch day's low. Widening it only shrinks the size.
wrong.No; cool off for a week first: The rule is a new trigger, not a waiting period. The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

questions.story: Stopped out of a launchpad on Tuesday. Thursday the stock closes back above all four averages, up 3%, on volume.
questions.simple: Yes, if the setup triggers again, as a fresh trade with its own stop and every rule checked.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stop. The new trade needs its own honest stop, a few cents under the new launch day's low. Widening it only means fewer shares. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: On daily bars the launch bar alone is the edge; the base and the stock are secondary.
questions.why: False. The launch bar looks the same on winners and losers. The stock, the base and the market are the edge, and the launch bar only times the entry. In the dossier's failures the launch bars matched the winners' bars.
questions.lesson_line: The bar times the trade. The stock, the base and the market decide it.
questions.simple: False, because the launch bar looks the same on winners and losers, so the stock, base and market carry the edge.

deeper.counter: A 2x launch bar was not a protection. TEAM closed up 4.1% on 2.13x volume and was stopped the next session. The failures had launch bars of +4.6% to +5.6% on 1.8x to 2.6x volume, just like the winners.

reasons: rests on proposed card lines (the bar is not the edge)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: Is this the launch?
choices: No; the day is under the 2% push
Yes; the close and volume carry it
Yes; above all four is enough
No; volume must reach 2x to count
questions.answer: No; the day is under the 2% push
questions.why: No. The launch bar is a real push, up 2% or more on the day. This bar was up 1.5%. Closing above all four averages is one test and the push is another, and the push failed. A strong close and 1.8x volume cannot replace the push.
questions.lesson_line: Every launch test has to pass. A quiet day above the averages is a wait.

wrong.Yes; the close and volume carry it: The close and the volume are separate tests. They do not make a 1.5% day a push.
wrong.Yes; above all four is enough: Above all four is one test. Up 2% or more is another, and it failed.
wrong.No; volume must reach 2x to count: 2x volume is the A+ version, not a rule. This bar fails on the 2% push, not on volume.

questions.story: A pad prints a +1.5% day that closes at 0.9 of its range on 1.8x volume, above all four averages.
questions.simple: No, because a launch must be up 2% or more on the day, and this bar was up only 1.5%.

reasons: the 2% push is a proposed card number

questions.q: Same pads otherwise. The 200-day is 9% under the bundle's middle on one, 12% under on the other. Which passes the 200-day test?
choices: The 9% pad only; within 10%
The 12% pad only; more room
Both; the line is within 15%
Neither; it must sit on the bundle
questions.why: The 9% pad only. The 200-day must be within 10% of the bundle's middle on the day before the launch. 9% passes. 12% is outside the line, so that 200-day is too far away. Better is at or just under the bundle, but that is a grade, not the gate.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day must sit within 10% of the bundle. Nine percent passes. Twelve does not.

wrong.The 12% pad only; more room: Room is not the point. 12% is outside the 10% line, so that 200-day is too far from the bundle.
wrong.Neither; it must sit on the bundle: The line is within 10%, not on the bundle. At or just under the bundle is the better grade, not the gate.
wrong.Both; the line is within 15%: The line is within 10%, not 15%. The 12% pad is outside it, so that 200-day is too far from the bundle.

questions.simple: The pad with the 200-day 9% away passes, because the line is within 10%. The 12% pad does not.

deeper.trap: Both pads look close, so it is easy to pass both. The line is a clean 10%: 9% is in and 12% is out. The card also calls at or just under the bundle better, but that is a grade, not the gate.

reasons: the 10% line for the 200-day is a proposed card number
reframed from a grade comparison to the gate (resolver)

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, earliest sell.
choices: Through the trigger; day-low stop; day 3
Limit below price; day-low stop; day 3
Next open; 200-day stop; day 1
At the close; day-low stop; day 3
questions.answer: Through the trigger; day-low stop; day 3
questions.why: Buy as price trades through the trigger during the day, with the stop a few cents under that day's low. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 at the earliest. We never buy at the close. Entries are market orders, so a limit below the market is not the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Know them before you buy and execute without a debate.

wrong.Next open; 200-day stop; day 1: The buy comes as price trades through the trigger, not at the next open. We very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Limit below price; day-low stop; day 3: Entries are market orders as price trades through the trigger, so a limit below the market is not the plan.
wrong.At the close; day-low stop; day 3: We never buy at the close. The buy comes as price trades through the trigger during the day.

questions.story: Weeks of closes under the bundle after a big fall. On the launch day it is up 3.6% and closes above all four.
questions.simple: Buy as price trades through the trigger, put the stop a few cents under the day's low, and sell no earlier than day 3.

deeper.trap: The trap is the entry and the stop. Buying at the close is never our way, and a stop far under the bundle or the base sits outside what we accept. Sizing from it gives a tiny position or a stop pulled in to fit. The primary stop is a few cents under the day's low.

reasons: rests on the adopted default for the entry (D-003 is held)
rests on the owner's rulebook (stop and trim rules)
fixed before (resolver)

questions.q: The day before a possible launch. Is this a launchpad to watch, or a pass?
choices: Watch it; weeks under the bundle
Pass; it rode on top of the averages
Pass; the 200-day is far away
Watch it; the pad is a flat base
questions.answer: Watch it; weeks under the bundle
questions.why: Watch it. The closes sat under a 0.7%-wide bundle for about two months, near a flat 200-day 4.9% away. That is the pad. The pad is the setup and the launch day is the trigger. The next day was the launch, up 3.8%, and the trade ran to 18.8R.
questions.lesson_line: Weeks under pinched averages, the 200-day close: that is the pad. Then wait for the launch.

wrong.Pass; it rode on top of the averages: Look again: the closes sat under the bundle for weeks, not on top of it.
wrong.Pass; the 200-day is far away: The 200-day sits 4.9% from the bundle here. That is inside the 10% line.
wrong.Watch it; the pad is a flat base: A flat base holds above the 50-day. These closes sat under the bundle.

questions.simple: Watch it, because the closes sat under the pinched averages for weeks, with the 200-day close by.

deeper.example: The test is where the closes sat, not how tight the lines look. Here about two months of closes sat under a 0.7%-wide bundle. Price riding on top of tight averages is a pullback breakout instead.

reasons: keys on the dossier's read of our own bars, not a public page
the count of closes under the bundle is held (D-062) and is not keyed

questions.q: Up 4.9% on 1.25x volume. Is it the launch? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; still under the 200-day
Take it; it cleared the bundle
Take it; 1.25x volume is enough
Pass; the volume is under 2x
questions.why: Pass. The launch bar must close above all four averages, and a close under the 200-day is not the launch. This bar closed at 148.03, above the 8, 21 and 50-day (top 146.83) but under the 200-day at 154.21. The bundle reclaim under a falling 200-day stopped on the way to the December low.
questions.lesson_line: Three of four is a reclaim. Four of four is the launch.

wrong.Take it; it cleared the bundle: Clearing the bundle is three of four. The 200-day sits above the close.
wrong.Take it; 1.25x volume is enough: Volume grades a launch. It does not put the close above the 200-day.
wrong.Pass; the volume is under 2x: 2x volume is the A+ version, not a rule. The pass is for the 200-day, which sits above the close.

questions.simple: Pass, because the bar closed under the 200-day, and a launch must close above all four averages.

deeper.trap: Three of four is a reclaim, not a launch. On the bar the close was 148.03. The top of the 8, 21 and 50-day was 146.83, and the 200-day sat at 154.21. The 200-day was falling after a 23% correction, and the stock was stopped on the way to the December low.

reasons: keys on the dossier's read of our own bars

questions.q: Haber waits or passes past a 3% stop. We prefer 1% to 3% but accept a stop up to 5% away.
questions.why: True. Haber: if the distance is more than 3%, the entry isn't there yet. Wait, or pass. We prefer 1% to 3%, call 3.5% good, and accept up to 5%. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. We never pull the stop in to fit.
questions.lesson_line: Haber passes past 3%. We prefer 1% to 3%, accept up to 5%, and never pull the stop in.
questions.simple: True. Haber waits past 3%, while we prefer 1% to 3% and accept up to 5%.

deeper.trap: Haber's 3% and ours are not the same line. His is a go or no-go on the entry: over 3% away, wait or pass. Ours is a range: 1% to 3% preferred, 3.5% good, up to 5% acceptable. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. Neither pulls the stop in to fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, A5, A3)
the stop-width habit is tied to a held decision (D-005)

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: Every other launchpad test passes. The launch bar is up 3.4%, closes at 0.85 of its range above all four averages, and trades 1.4x the 50-day volume. The reading is Green.
choices: Take it; volume only lifts the grade
Pass; a launch needs 2x volume to count
Pass; wait for a 2x day to follow
Take it; sell day one if volume fades
questions.answer: Take it; volume only lifts the grade
questions.why: Take it. Volume of 2 times the 50-day average or more is the A+ version of the launch bar, not a rule. This bar has 1.4x, so it grades lower, not out. The push, the close and the four averages all pass. Heavy volume is no protection either: TEAM was up 4.1% on 2.13x volume and was stopped the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Volume lifts the grade. It is not a gate, and it is no protection.
questions.simple: Take it. Heavy volume lifts the grade, but lighter volume does not stop the launch from counting.

wrong.Pass; a launch needs 2x volume to count: 2x volume is the A+ version of the launch bar, not a rule. This bar passes on its push, its close and the four averages.
wrong.Pass; wait for a 2x day to follow: Waiting for volume is not a test. Volume grades the bar and does not gate it, and a 2x launch bar did not protect TEAM.
wrong.Take it; sell day one if volume fades: We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The stop is the exit, not a volume read.
